name: Co-amoxiclav (Augmentin)
summary: A penicillin antibiotic that combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, used for bacterial infections such as those of the skin and ears. It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to it or another antibiotic, or liver problems or jaundice from an antibiotic. The NHS lists diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush as common side effects.
class: Penicillin antibiotic with a beta-lactamase inhibitor
usedFor: Bacterial skin and ear infections, the uses the NHS highlights.
Sinus, chest, urinary, dental, and bone and joint infections, according to UK patient leaflets.
Infections of the ears, lungs, sinuses, skin and urinary tract, as listed by MedlinePlus.
howItWorks: Co-amoxiclav is an antibiotic that works by killing the bacteria causing an infection. It contains two medicines, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. MedlinePlus describes amoxicillin as a penicillin-like antibiotic and clavulanic acid as a beta-lactamase inhibitor. Dental prescribing guidance describes the combination as active against beta-lactamase-producing bacteria that are resistant to amoxicillin.

common: Diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush are the common side effects listed by the NHS.
The NHS says co-amoxiclav will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery.
Rash, itching and headache are listed as uncommon in UK patient leaflets.
serious: Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, can cause swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or very fast or difficult breathing, and needs a 999 call.
Serious skin reactions include a rash with blisters or peeling skin, or a rash around the bottom, inner thighs, armpits and neck; NHS 111 is the route if serious side effects are suspected.
Liver problems can show as pale poo with dark pee, or yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin (jaundice), and call for NHS 111 or the GP the same day.
Severe diarrhoea, especially watery diarrhoea with blood or mucus, stomach pain or fever, can mean serious bowel inflammation, and UK patient leaflets say to contact a doctor.
Pancreatitis causes severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away, and needs NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

cautions: The NHS says most adults and children can take co-amoxiclav, but it is not suitable for everyone.

It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to co-amoxiclav or another antibiotic, which can include a skin rash or swelling of the face and throat; UK leaflets also list allergy to penicillins.
It is not suitable for people who have had liver problems or jaundice from an antibiotic before, and MedlinePlus asks that past liver problems be reported to the doctor.
UK patient leaflets list glandular fever, kidney problems, liver problems and not passing urine regularly as reasons to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says co-amoxiclav can usually be used in pregnancy if the doctor thinks it is needed, and usually while breastfeeding after checking with a pharmacist or doctor.
The NHS names gout medicines such as allopurinol or probenecid, warfarin and methotrexate as medicines that may not mix well with it.

A 2026 NHS Somerset primary care guide advises avoiding broad-spectrum antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav when narrower ones remain effective, because they raise the risk of C. difficile, MRSA and resistant urinary infections.
monitoring: UK patient information says that for people with kidney or liver problems the prescriber may change the treatment or arrange extra blood tests.
regimenNote: Taken by mouth as tablets or a liquid, according to the NHS; MedlinePlus also lists chewable tablets.

sections.heading: What is co-amoxiclav used for?
sections.body: Co-amoxiclav is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats infections caused by bacteria. The NHS describes it as a penicillin antibiotic that can be used to treat skin or ear infections. UK patient leaflets list a wider range, including sinus, chest, urinary, dental, and bone and joint infections. MedlinePlus gives a similar list, naming infections of the ears, lungs, sinuses, skin and urinary tract. The NHS says most adults and children can take it, although it is not suitable for everyone. It usually comes as tablets or a liquid taken by mouth, and MedlinePlus also lists a chewable tablet. Local prescribing guidance for England advises avoiding broad-spectrum antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav when narrower ones remain effective. The reason given is that broader antibiotics increase the risk of Clostridium difficile infection, MRSA and urinary infections that resist treatment.

sections.heading: How does co-amoxiclav work?
sections.body: Co-amoxiclav contains two medicines, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. The leaflets explain that together they work by killing the bacteria that cause the infection. MedlinePlus describes amoxicillin as a penicillin-like antibiotic. It describes clavulanic acid as a beta-lactamase inhibitor. Dental prescribing guidance describes the combination as active against beta-lactamase-producing bacteria that are resistant to amoxicillin. Because co-amoxiclav covers a wider range of bacteria, the primary care guide mentioned earlier groups it with broad-spectrum antibiotics. The NHS describes co-amoxiclav as a penicillin antibiotic, and MedlinePlus describes the combination as a penicillin-like antibiotic with a beta-lactamase inhibitor. MedlinePlus lists tablets, chewable tablets and an oral suspension, which is a liquid form, among the available forms. Product leaflets from the UK electronic medicines compendium name the same two ingredients across tablets and other forms of co-amoxiclav.

sections.heading: What are the common side effects?
sections.body: The NHS lists diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush as the common side effects of co-amoxiclav. It also says co-amoxiclav will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery. UK patient leaflets place rash, itching and headache in the uncommon group. Serious side effects are described by the NHS as rare. MedlinePlus lists severe vomiting as a warning sign to report to the doctor. The leaflets note that frequencies vary slightly between products, so the leaflet in the pack is the reference for a particular medicine. The emc leaflets also place inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord in an unknown-frequency group, and say a severe rash, blistering or a serious allergic reaction needs a doctor straight away.

sections.heading: Which warning signs need urgent help?
sections.body: The NHS lists four serious side effects: anaphylaxis, skin reactions, liver problems and pancreatitis. Anaphylaxis can cause sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or difficult breathing, and calling 999 is the route for this emergency. A penicillin allergy can also show as a skin rash or swelling of the face and throat, which the leaflets say to report to a doctor immediately. Serious skin reactions include a rash with blisters or peeling skin. Liver problems can show as pale poo with dark pee, or yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin, and NHS 111 or the GP the same day is the route. Pancreatitis causes severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away. Severe diarrhoea, particularly watery diarrhoea with blood or mucus, stomach pain or fever, can mean serious bowel inflammation, and UK leaflets say to contact a doctor. The NHS advises calling NHS 111 for anyone taking co-amoxiclav who thinks serious side effects may be happening.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and which medicines interact?
sections.body: People who have had an allergic reaction to co-amoxiclav or another antibiotic are among those the NHS says it is not suitable for. The same applies to people who have had liver problems or jaundice from an antibiotic before. UK leaflets list glandular fever, kidney problems, liver problems and not passing urine regularly as reasons to talk to a doctor or pharmacist before taking it. MedlinePlus asks that any past liver problems be reported to the doctor. In pregnancy the NHS says co-amoxiclav can usually be used if the doctor thinks it is needed. While breastfeeding it is usually fine to take after checking with a pharmacist or doctor. The NHS names gout medicines such as allopurinol or probenecid, warfarin and methotrexate as medicines that may not mix well with it. Anyone taking other medicines, herbal remedies or supplements is advised in the leaflets to tell the prescriber.

faqs.q: Is co-amoxiclav the same as amoxicillin?
faqs.a: No. Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin together with a second medicine, clavulanic acid, which MedlinePlus describes as a beta-lactamase inhibitor. Dental guidance describes the combination as active against bacteria that make beta-lactamase and resist amoxicillin on its own.

faqs.q: What are the common side effects of co-amoxiclav?
faqs.a: The NHS lists diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush as the common ones. The NHS says co-amoxiclav will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery, and serious side effects are rare.

The NHS lists liver problems among the rare serious side effects, with pale poo and dark pee or yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes as signs. It is not suitable for people who have had liver problems or jaundice from an antibiotic before. NHS 111 or the GP the same day is the route.

faqs.q: What if the face or throat swells after taking it?
faqs.a: Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or difficult breathing, may be anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, and the NHS route is to call 999. UK leaflets also list facial or throat swelling that makes breathing hard as a sign to get help immediately.

faqs.q: Can co-amoxiclav be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can usually be used in pregnancy if the doctor thinks it is needed, and usually while breastfeeding after checking with a pharmacist or doctor. Individual questions about this are for a pharmacist, midwife or prescriber.
